claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance in refractory multiprincipal-element alloys is governed by rapid formation of a continuous protective oxide layer.
Cr2O3 and Al2O3 can act as protective oxide barriers in high-temperature alloys.
Cr2O3 has a compact structure and superior oxidation resistance.
Protective oxide formation occurs through selective, accelerated diffusion of key oxide-forming elements.
Failure to form a protective oxide layer permits outward Mn migration and formation of Mn3O4.
Mn3O4 is a less protective oxide that compromises alloy integrity.
The continuity and compactness of the surface oxide scale mediate oxidation resistance.
Surface and grain-boundary diffusion kinetics mediate formation of the protective oxide scale.
High temperature promotes selective outward diffusion of oxide-forming elements, causing nucleation and growth of a protective oxide layer.
A rapidly formed continuous protective layer suppresses further oxidation by limiting diffusion of less oxidation-stable elements.
Increasing Cr and/or Al concentration will cause more rapid formation of a continuous, dense protective oxide scale than in a lower-Cr/Al baseline.
The higher-Cr/Al alloy will exhibit lower oxidation weight gain than the baseline alloy.
The higher-Cr/Al alloy will retain better microstructural integrity than the baseline alloy.
An alloy with insufficient oxide-forming elements will develop a discontinuous, less protective scale and undergo accelerated degradation.
The proposed governing behavior applies to refractory multiprincipal-element alloys oxidized in air between 900 and 1000 degrees Celsius.
The proposed behavior may not apply at substantially lower temperatures, in highly reducing environments, or in drastically different alloy chemistries.
Refractory multiprincipal-element alloys are candidate materials for demanding high-temperature applications.
